title: Therapeutic reset of the mutant epidermal field

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that selectively eliminates or outcompetes cancer-promoting mutant cell clones across a field of skin, preserves functioning epidermis, and leaves a durable reduction in subsequent cancer risk. A clone is a population descended from a cell carrying particular mutations. Sun-exposed skin can contain many such populations even where it looks and functions normally, so the treatment would address an underlying cellular reservoir extending beyond visible lesions.

In this proposed definition, a reset would require both representative tissue measurements showing sustained depletion of the targeted clones and controlled evidence of fewer cancers of the targeted type. Clearing actinic keratoses, reducing the number of detected mutations briefly, or treating individual cancers would provide useful evidence but would not alone establish the complete capability. The goal is a lower cancer-relevant mutant burden compatible with healthy skin, rather than removal of every mutated cell or restoration of a literally mutation-free epidermis.

significance.text: A safe, durable reset could make prevention operate across a cancer-prone tissue field rather than repeatedly responding to lesions as they appear. The biological rationale is strongest for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma: mutations under positive selection in normal sun-exposed epidermis substantially overlap those implicated in this cancer. Existing field treatments can already eliminate actinic keratoses and early keratinocyte cancers and reduce cancer risk; the proposed advance would add selective, molecularly verified and durable modification of the underlying field.

The direct molecular consequence would be fewer cells belonging to the targeted cancer-promoting clones. Fewer actinic keratoses and squamous cell carcinomas are plausible clinical benefits that would still need demonstration. A fall in aggregate driver-mutation burden is not sufficient proof: mutations differ in malignant potential, clone size need not track transformation risk, and many cells carrying cancer-associated mutations continue to support normal tissue function. The 2025 Nature Communications study also describes transformation as a multistep process requiring additional drivers, rather than an inevitable outcome of a TP53 or NOTCH1 mutation.

Conditional downstream possibilities include fewer repeated procedures and a lower cumulative treatment burden for people with extensive sun damage, many previous cancers or transplant-associated risk. Those benefits would depend on the magnitude and duration of cancer prevention, treatment tolerability and the ability to treat substantial skin areas. The evidence supporting the field rationale does not establish comparable prevention of basal cell carcinoma or melanoma: the 2015 study found much less overlap with their positively selected genes. Benefits across those diseases would require separate evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability in the supplied evidence is selective, durable depletion of cancer-promoting epidermal clones, followed by fewer cancers while preserving epidermal function. Selection is a central difficulty because cancer-associated mutations are already widespread in physiologically normal skin. The 2015 study specifically raises the possibility of collateral damage from targeting NOTCH1-inactivated cells. A successful intervention would therefore need to discriminate clinically consequential populations well enough to avoid damaging large amounts of useful epidermis merely because it carries a mutation associated with cancer.

Durability presents a separate barrier. The human photodynamic-therapy evidence measures an effect approximately one month after treatment, predominantly among low-frequency clonal mutations. It does not establish sustained depletion of persistent cancer-promoting populations or how the treated field subsequently repopulates. The 2025 study proposes investigating whether immunotherapies can eliminate precancerous cells prophylactically, but that suggestion is a research direction rather than a demonstrated solution.

As an engineering and measurement synthesis, a convincing reset must solve several linked problems: identify which clones matter for future cancer, reach them throughout a heterogeneous field, permit safe tissue renewal, and measure whether the replacement population remains less cancer-prone. Sequencing must distinguish numbers of detected mutations from clone abundance and from cancer-relevant driver burden. Variant allele frequency—the fraction of sequencing reads carrying a variant—also requires interpretation in light of tissue composition and copy number. Molecular changes must ultimately be linked to clinical outcomes rather than treated as a sufficient surrogate.

current_state.text: In the Science study published on 22 May 2015, Martincorena and colleagues sequenced 234 biopsies of sun-exposed eyelid epidermis from four individuals. They estimated that 18–32% of normal skin cells carried positively selected driver mutations, with approximately 140 driver mutations per square centimeter, despite retained physiological function. These estimates concern the sampled older donors' eyelid epidermis; they should not be generalized numerically to all normal skin. The findings establish a substantial mutant field, not that every mutation-bearing cell is precancerous or should be removed.

Wei and colleagues' British Journal of Dermatology study, dated 27 August 2024 in the supplied research, provides an early human molecular treatment result. In five patients sampled before and 31–35 days after photodynamic therapy, median detected clonal-mutation counts fell from 188 per sample, with a range of 52–418, to 151, with a range of 45–277 (P = 0.02). The difference was predominantly attributable to low-variant-allele-frequency mutations. Counts of mutations above 1% variant allele frequency did not decrease significantly (P = 0.20); this does not prove that treatment had zero effect on those populations. These are mutation-count findings, not demonstrated selective eradication of driver clones, long-term field restoration or linked reductions in subsequent cancers.

Tandukar and colleagues' Nature Communications article, published on 27 November 2025, reports substantially greater mutation burdens in keratinocytes carrying TP53 or NOTCH1 mutations. Its results include 137 keratinocyte single-cell expansions from a broader biopsy cohort. The authors suggest that these mutations may prime cells for transformation by increasing mutation rates, with additional driver mutations still needed. The culture-based approach may introduce selection bias, and the comparison should not be described as a direct comparison between each mutant cell and its physical neighbors. The article proposes prophylactic immunotherapy research but does not demonstrate a clinical field reset.

The supplied review establishes that the Nature article was available as full open-access HTML and a full 17-page article PDF, correcting the earlier description of abstract-only access after a paywall redirect. Its principal findings therefore do not rest on an abstract alone. Review coverage still has limits: separate supplements and figure images for the 2015 study were not inspected, and a retained Nature supplementary PDF had pages without extractable text. No additional findings from those materials are assumed here.

Taken together, the supplied evidence establishes the biological rationale and a short-term molecular response to photodynamic therapy, but does not demonstrate the proposed selective, durable reset with subsequent cancer prevention. The supplied materials do not verify the earlier checkpoint-inhibitor pilot details or the claim that nicotinamide's preventive benefit stops after cessation; those assertions remain unconfirmed here, rather than disproven. Because no bounded freshness search record was supplied, these materials also cannot establish whether the complete capability remained unavailable as of 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: conduct a controlled trial in a defined high-risk population, such as organ-transplant recipients or people with many previous keratinocyte cancers. Pre-specify the targeted cancer type and what constitutes a substantial reduction in cancer-relevant driver-mutant burden. Representative tissue sequencing months after treatment should show that reduction, with persistence for at least two years, accompanied by a pre-specified reduction in new cancers of the targeted type over three to five years. These durations and thresholds are proposed criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: ≥2-year driver-burden reduction accompanies fewer targeted cancers over 3–5 years

completion_criteria.text: Proposed molecular validation: sample sufficiently across the treated field to distinguish a field-wide response from a favorable biopsy location, and distinguish clone abundance, mutation counts and risk-relevant driver burden. Interpret allele-frequency changes with tissue composition and copy number in view. Repeated measurements should establish sustained depletion rather than a transient change in detection. Short-term actinic-keratosis clearance alone would not meet the proposed endpoint, and a molecular response without fewer cancers would establish only part of the intended capability.
completion_criteria.label: Representative field-wide sampling confirms sustained depletion of risk-relevant mutant drivers

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety and reproducibility requirements: demonstrate preserved epidermal function, acceptable local and systemic toxicity, and feasible treatment of clinically useful skin areas without requiring additional chronic systemic immunosuppression. This wording permits transplant recipients to continue necessary maintenance immunosuppression. Replication across independent investigators, treatment settings and relevant patient groups should define where the intervention works and where it does not. Finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth for specified populations, skin sites and cancer types, not universal protection against skin cancer.
completion_criteria.label: Safe, feasible treatment preserves epidermal function across independently replicated settings

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison with DER-05, Epidermal DNA repair sufficient to prevent ultraviolet-driven skin cancer: preventing new UV-driven mutations and reducing established mutant populations address different stages of carcinogenesis and could be complementary. Repairing DNA damage prospectively would not, by itself, establish removal of decades-old clones. Only DER-05's title and the candidate's comparison were supplied, so its actual demonstrated capabilities cannot be assessed here.

Roster-based comparison with DER-02, One-time genomic cure of severe monogenic skin disease through the epidermal stem-cell compartment, and DER-04, Programmable passage of macromolecules and gene editors across intact stratum corneum: DER-02 concerns correcting an inherited disease through its sustaining cell compartment, whereas DER-06 concerns a heterogeneous acquired mutant field. DER-04 could enable delivery of a reset therapy, but delivery across the barrier would not itself demonstrate selective clone depletion, durability or cancer prevention. These remain distinct innovations.

Roster-based comparison with DER-03, Antigen-selective erasure of pathogenic cutaneous immune memory: both concepts require selective removal of a harmful cellular population while preserving useful tissue functions, but DER-03 targets pathogenic immune memory and DER-06 targets cancer-promoting epidermal clones. Immunotherapy could nevertheless be a mechanism for DER-06. The Nature study explicitly proposes investigating prophylactic elimination of precancerous cells; a vaccine could also qualify if it achieved the same molecular, functional and clinical endpoints. The supplied evidence does not support excluding vaccination by asserting that no shared preventive antigen exists.

Roster-based comparison with DER-01, Clinical restoration of a complete human skin organ, and DER-08, Reconstitution of melanocyte stem cells where the follicular reservoir is gone: these concern restoring an organ or a lost cellular reservoir. DER-06 instead seeks to alter the clonal composition of epidermis that may already function normally. Regeneration might contribute to safe repopulation after treatment, but organ restoration or pigment-cell replacement would not independently establish a cancer-preventive field reset.

Roster-based comparison with DER-07, A skin-origin intervention that prevents atopic dermatitis and the atopic march, DER-09, Durable regenerative closure of diabetic foot ulcers after ischemia and pressure are treated, and DER-10, In situ reversal of established keloids and pathological cutaneous scars: all seek lasting changes in skin biology, but their endpoints concern allergic disease prevention, wound closure and scar reversal, respectively. Their success would not demonstrate depletion of cancer-promoting epidermal clones, and DER-06 would not establish those outcomes. These distinctions follow from the supplied titles; detailed records for those concepts were not provided.

unresolved_issues: Whether a selective, durable molecular field reset with controlled cancer-prevention outcomes had been demonstrated by 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because no bounded freshness search record was supplied.
Which mutations and clonal configurations should determine cancer-relevant burden, and how much their depletion must change cancer risk, remain open questions.

The earlier JAMA Dermatology checkpoint-pilot assertion—mean actinic-keratosis counts falling from 47.2 to 14.3 at 12 months—its quoted premise and its toxicity/cost conclusions lack supplied source text. PMC11570346 supports the PDT study, not that pilot; the assertions are unverified rather than disproven.
The claim that nicotinamide's preventive benefit stops after treatment cessation lacks supplied supporting text.
Long-term persistence, safe repopulation and subsequent cancer outcomes after the reported PDT molecular response are not established by the supplied study.
Benefits for basal cell carcinoma or melanoma, and the availability of suitable preventive vaccine antigens, require separate evidence.
Detailed records for the other roster entries were not supplied, so their mechanisms, maturity and precise overlap cannot be established beyond the stated conceptual comparisons.

Separate supplements and figure images for the 2015 study were outside the supplied review's inspection, and one Nature supplementary PDF had poorly extractable pages; no conclusions from those unreviewed contents were assumed.

brief.title: Lasting skin cancer prevention across sun-damaged skin
possible: People with sun-damaged skin could receive treatment across an area, including skin that looks normal, to reduce future cancer risk. It would selectively remove or outcompete cancer-promoting clones—groups of cells descended from a mutated cell—while keeping the skin working normally.
why: For people facing repeated skin cancers, including transplant recipients, lasting prevention could mean fewer procedures and less treatment. It would address the cells that can give rise to cancers across sun-damaged skin.
The strongest case concerns squamous cell carcinoma, a cancer of the skin’s outer layer. Many mutations that help cells spread through apparently normal skin also occur in this cancer.

sources.showed: Apparently normal, sun-exposed eyelid skin contained many clones carrying mutations associated with cancer. The study involved four older donors whose skin retained normal function.
sources.quote: Thus, aged, sun-exposed skin is a patchwork of thousands of evolving clones, with over a quarter of cells carrying cancer-causing mutations while maintaining the physiological functions of epidermis.
sources.cited_for: Cancer-associated mutations extend beyond visible skin lesions.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish which clones need removal or whether removing them would prevent cancer safely.

sources.who: Bishal Tandukar, Delahny Deivendran and colleagues
sources.showed: Skin cells carrying mutations in the TP53 or NOTCH1 genes had higher mutation burdens. Growing cells in culture before measuring them may have biased which cells were studied.

sources.cited_for: Some cancer-associated mutations accompany a greater accumulation of mutations in skin cells.
sources.not_established: The study did not test a treatment that selectively removes these cells or prevents subsequent cancers.

sources.showed: Photodynamic therapy, a light-based treatment, reduced detected mutations mainly among those present at low frequencies. Human measurements came about a month after treatment.
sources.quote: By comparing skin before and after PDT in five patients and a mouse model of chronic UV carcinogenesis, a significant reduction in low-frequency mutations post-treatment was revealed.
sources.cited_for: Treatment can produce a short-term molecular change in sun-damaged skin.
sources.not_established: The study did not demonstrate selective removal of cancer-promoting clones, lasting depletion or fewer subsequent cancers.

shown: Wei and colleagues provide an early treatment result: detected mutations fell after light-based therapy in five patients, mainly among mutations present at low frequencies. This is a short-term molecular response; a lasting reduction in cancer-promoting clones linked to fewer cancers remains unestablished.
missing: A treatment must selectively deplete cancer-promoting clones across the treated area while preserving useful skin cells.
The reduction must persist as skin renews itself, with the replacement cells remaining less cancer-prone.
Controlled trials must connect the molecular change to fewer cancers of the targeted type.

milestones.label: Lasting depletion accompanies fewer targeted cancers
milestones.explanation: A controlled trial would have to show depletion of cancer-promoting clones lasting at least two years alongside fewer targeted cancers over longer follow-up. This would connect lasting cellular change to prevention.

milestones.label: Sampling confirms lasting depletion across the treated area
milestones.explanation: Repeated samples across the area would have to distinguish lasting loss of cancer-promoting clones from changes in detected mutation counts. This would establish that the response extends beyond a favorable sampling spot.

milestones.label: Safe, practical treatment works independently
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to preserve skin function across useful areas without added long-term suppression of immunity throughout the body. Acceptable toxicity and repeatable results would establish practical use.

uncertain: Which mutations and combinations of clones best predict future cancer, and how much must their abundance fall to reduce risk?
Can skin safely repopulate after treatment without rebuilding the same cancer-prone cell populations?
Whether this approach could prevent basal cell carcinoma or melanoma requires separate evidence.

page.title: Selective depletion of cancer-promoting epidermal clones
page.definition: A treatment selectively depletes cancer-promoting clones—cell populations descended from a mutated cell—across sun-damaged epidermis, the skin’s outer layer. Depletion persists after treatment, the epidermis retains its barrier function, and controlled human evidence shows fewer new invasive cutaneous squamous-cell carcinomas.

goal.need: Among 624 people treated for at least five actinic keratoses on the head, the four-year risk of invasive squamous-cell carcinoma in the treated area was 3.7%. Treating visible lesions leaves genetically altered cells in the surrounding skin. In high-risk veterans, fluorouracil reduced the need for SCC surgery on the face or ears during the first year. The four-year trial found no overall reduction in SCC risk. Lasting protection could spare patients further surgery if treatment reaches cancer-promoting clones while preserving the skin’s barrier.

completion.title: A controlled human study shows persistent driver-clone depletion and fewer invasive skin cSCCs.
completion.criterion: After a finite field treatment, a controlled human study meets prospectively specified efficacy endpoints for both selective depletion of cancer-promoting epidermal clones and fewer histologically confirmed new invasive cSCCs in the treated field. Genotype-resolved sampling establishes depletion after healing and its persistence through cancer follow-up; epidermal-function assessments establish retained barrier function. The protocol specifies effect sizes, follow-up, sampling and safety limits. No universal numerical threshold for this combined capability was found.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; fallback synthesis of the NCI-funded molecular-prevention goal and professional-society cancer-prevention goal.
completion.basis: Searches of NCI prevention goals, AAD and European field-cancerization guidelines, ClinicalTrials.gov records and molecular-treatment papers found no combined definition specifying clone depletion, persistence, cancer reduction and epidermal function. The NCI-funded project studies reductions in mutations and cancer formation; the European guideline targets invasive cSCC prevention. This fallback joins those outcomes without assigning an unsupported percentage or duration.

milestones.title: A field treatment reduces epidermal mutations below 1% variant allele frequency in UVB-exposed mice.
milestones.criterion: After eight weeks of UVB exposure at 120 mJ/cm² three times weekly, use targeted sequencing to count epidermal mutations present in less than 1% of reads at the affected site. The count per sample must be significantly lower in treated skin than in both the untreated opposite side of the same mice and untreated skin from separately irradiated mice.
milestones.set_by: Wei et al., published mouse experiment and Figure 1d; study-specific comparison.

milestones.title: Human epidermis has fewer mutations below 1% variant allele frequency 31–35 days after field treatment.
milestones.criterion: Sample clinically normal-appearing skin in the same sun-damaged treatment field before treatment and 31–35 days afterward. Use targeted sequencing of equal-area epidermal samples to show a significant decrease in the number of mutations per sample present in less than 1% of reads at the affected site.
milestones.set_by: Wei et al., published human study and Figure 1b; study-specific comparison.
milestones.threshold_quote: before and 31–35 days after PDT from clinically healthy-appearing skin

milestones.title: A field treatment lowers first-year risk of SCC requiring surgery on the face or ears.
milestones.criterion: In a randomized comparison with vehicle cream, show a lower proportion of participants with at least one primary, histologically confirmed SCC removed surgically from the face or ears during the first year after enrollment. Count participants with an event, regardless of how many tumors each has removed.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Veterans Affairs, VAKCC trial NCT00847912, prespecified first-year cancer outcomes.
milestones.threshold_quote: Other key a priori outcomes were risk of BCC, SCC, and KC in the first year after enrollment.

milestones.title: A short field treatment lowers three-year risk of SCC, including in situ disease, on the face or scalp.
milestones.criterion: In immunocompetent participants followed after randomized field treatment, compare the proportions with at least one histologically diagnosed primary SCC on the treated face or scalp within three years of trial initiation. Count both invasive and in situ SCC. The proportion must be lower in the treatment group at P < 0.05.
milestones.set_by: Rosenberg et al., blinded prospective cohort follow-up of the randomized actinic-keratosis trial.
milestones.threshold_quote: primary SCC (including invasive and in situ lesions)

milestones.title: Cancer-promoting epidermal clones remain selectively depleted through clinical follow-up.
milestones.criterion: After a finite field treatment, use genotype-resolved sampling to show that prespecified cancer-promoting clones occupy less epidermis than at baseline and in control fields. Compare the change with that of prespecified nontarget epidermal populations to establish preferential depletion. Demonstrate both effects after healing and at the final cancer follow-up, with retained barrier function. Prespecify effect sizes, sampling times and functional safety limits.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback. No external protocol was found that defines persistent selective depletion of cancer-promoting epidermal clones together with retained barrier function.

milestones.title: A field treatment reduces the density of mutant-p53-staining patches in UVB-exposed mouse epidermis.
milestones.criterion: After UVB exposure stops, compare treated mice with vehicle controls at matched times. Count patches per square centimetre of epidermal sheet, scoring a patch when more than eight adjacent cells stain with the Pab240 antibody to mutant p53. The treated group must have fewer stained patches per unit area.
milestones.set_by: Lu et al., mouse experiment and Table I.
milestones.threshold_quote: Number of patches of mutant p53 positive cells/cm²/mouse

milestones.title: A randomized field-treatment trial measures three-year incidence of biopsy-confirmed invasive SCC.
milestones.criterion: Compare the three-year cumulative incidence of biopsy-confirmed invasive cutaneous SCC in the defined face or scalp treatment field between randomized treatment groups. Use time to first invasive SCC or censoring. Exclude SCC in situ from the primary endpoint.
milestones.set_by: LEO Pharma A/S, registered phase 4 comparative safety protocol LP0041-63, NCT01926496.
milestones.threshold_quote: invasive SCC i.e. excludes SCC in situ) in the treatment field across the 3-year trial period.

not_found: No registered human protocol was located with both persistent genotype-specific epidermal clone depletion and invasive-cSCC prevention as efficacy endpoints.
The full text of the 2026 paper comparing fluorouracil and photodynamic therapy could not be opened; its results were not used.
No human field-treatment study was found that demonstrated preferential depletion of genotype-defined cancer-promoting clones through cancer follow-up with retained epidermal barrier function.

goal.need = "Among 624 people treated for at least five actinic keratoses on the head, the four-year risk of invasive squamous-cell carcinoma in the treated area was 3.7%. Treating visible lesions leaves genetically altered cells in the surrounding skin. In high-risk veterans, fluorouracil reduced the need for SCC surgery on the face or ears during the first year. The four-year trial found no overall reduction in SCC risk. Lasting protection could spare patients further surgery if treatment reaches cancer-promoting clones while preserving the skin\u2019s barrier.". Reason: The current rationale describes sequencing samples and refers to a burden “shown below” without telling patients how often invasive cancer occurs after treatment or what prevention could spare them.

add milestone after None: "A field treatment reduces the density of mutant-p53-staining patches in UVB-exposed mouse epidermis.". Reason: The 2005 mouse experiment supplies an early field-treatment test that distinguishes disappearance of a mutant-protein marker from demonstrated loss of the cells carrying the mutation.

edit m1: title = "A field treatment reduces epidermal mutations below 1% variant allele frequency in UVB-exposed mice."; criterion = "After eight weeks of UVB exposure at 120 mJ/cm\u00b2 three times weekly, use targeted sequencing to count epidermal mutations present in less than 1% of reads at the affected site. The count per sample must be significantly lower in treated skin than in both the untreated opposite side of the same mice and untreated skin from separately irradiated mice."; threshold_quote = "significantly fewer low VAF mutations"; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6]. Reason: The mouse criterion embeds sample counts and observed effects where it needs to specify the mutation-frequency cutoff and the two untreated comparisons.

edit m2: title = "Human epidermis has fewer mutations below 1% variant allele frequency 31\u201335 days after field treatment."; criterion = "Sample clinically normal-appearing skin in the same sun-damaged treatment field before treatment and 31\u201335 days afterward. Use targeted sequencing of equal-area epidermal samples to show a significant decrease in the number of mutations per sample present in less than 1% of reads at the affected site."; threshold_quote = "before and 31\u201335\u2005days after PDT from clinically healthy-appearing skin"; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6]. Reason: The human criterion mixes the test with the five-patient result and can be made explicit about the sampled tissue, frequency cutoff and timing.

edit m3: title = "A field treatment lowers first-year risk of SCC requiring surgery on the face or ears."; criterion = "In a randomized comparison with vehicle cream, show a lower proportion of participants with at least one primary, histologically confirmed SCC removed surgically from the face or ears during the first year after enrollment. Count participants with an event, regardless of how many tumors each has removed."; threshold_quote = "Other key a priori outcomes were risk of BCC, SCC, and KC in the first year after enrollment."; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7]. Reason: The observed risk ratio and event counts obscure that the prespecified outcome was a participant’s first-year risk of a surgically treated SCC at the treated sites.

edit m4: title = "A short field treatment lowers three-year risk of SCC, including in situ disease, on the face or scalp."; criterion = "In immunocompetent participants followed after randomized field treatment, compare the proportions with at least one histologically diagnosed primary SCC on the treated face or scalp within three years of trial initiation. Count both invasive and in situ SCC. The proportion must be lower in the treatment group at P < 0.05."; set_by = "Rosenberg et al., blinded prospective cohort follow-up of the randomized actinic-keratosis trial."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "primary SCC (including invasive and in situ lesions)"; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [8]. Reason: The title conceals the combined invasive and in situ endpoint, and the criterion and attribution include the observed result.

add milestone after m4: "A randomized field-treatment trial measures three-year incidence of biopsy-confirmed invasive SCC.". Reason: A registered phase 4 protocol supplies a missing clinical stage that measures invasive SCC separately from in situ disease at the site of treatment.

edit m5: criterion = "After a finite field treatment, use genotype-resolved sampling to show that prespecified cancer-promoting clones occupy less epidermis than at baseline and in control fields. Compare the change with that of prespecified nontarget epidermal populations to establish preferential depletion. Demonstrate both effects after healing and at the final cancer follow-up, with retained barrier function. Prespecify effect sizes, sampling times and functional safety limits."; set_by = "Technology Atlas fallback. No external protocol was found that defines persistent selective depletion of cancer-promoting epidermal clones together with retained barrier function."; set_by_kind = "atlas"; refs = [1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 12]. Reason: Epidermal ablation can lower mutation burden after regrowth, so selectivity requires a comparison with nontarget epidermal populations as well as with untreated skin.
